headline: Overnight, the AI-credit rout took over from hot CPI as the driver: CoreWeave CDS is above 1,000 bp and the Kospi fell 7.6%, and the bid for safety has pulled the 10Y down ≈9 bp to ≈5.10% and cut Oct 28 hike odds to roughly a third. PPI and retail sales at 7:30 CT decide whether inflation or the flight to quality sets the front end.
summary: Correction to yesterday's Close update: its tiles (2Y ≈4.90%, 10Y ≈5.29%) were the post-CPI intraday spike, not the close. CNBC's closes were 2Y 4.81% (+1 bp), 10Y 5.19% (−2 bp) and 30Y 5.52% (−4 bp), after the 10Y touched ≈5.33%. The curve bear-flattened on CPI (core +0.3% m/m, 2.6% y/y), then bull-steepened when tech broke and shorts covered. This morning the 2Y is 4.74% (−6 bp), the 10Y 5.10% (−9 bp, a three-week low) and the 30Y 5.44%.

The risk-off is about AI credit, not just tech multiples. CoreWeave fell 15% Wednesday and is ≈−4.5% pre-market, its 2032 bonds yield above 15%, and its CDS widened from >600 bp to >1,000 bp. CNBC tallies more than $1T lost this week across the top 20 AI/chip names, and the Kospi closed −7.6% after a circuit breaker (SK Hynix and Samsung each fell >11%) even though TSMC beat (ADR EPS $4.60 vs ≈$4.44; Q4 guide $52.3–54.3B). NQ futures are ≈−1.2%, ES ≈−0.4% and Dow futures ≈+0.4%.

7:30 CT: PPI (Sep) consensus is +0.5% m/m (some surveys say +0.6%) with core at +0.3%. Retail sales are seen at +0.3% (prior +1.2%), ex-autos at +0.5%, and claims at 195K. A hot core PPI feeds straight into core PCE and would undo the overnight rally. Hike odds for Oct 28 swung from >50% intraday Wednesday to ≈30–37% late, December is ≈90%, and Commerzbank counts ≈29 bp of hikes by end-2026 and ≈75 bp by end-2027.

Regional banks are beating on EPS and slightly missing on revenue. PNC posted adjusted EPS of $5.09 vs $4.91 and revenue of $6.56B vs $6.61B; NII was $4.2B (+$99M q/q), average loans rose 17% y/y on C&I, and net charge-offs were up 44% y/y to $257M. USB posted $1.34 vs $1.32, revenue $7.97B vs $8.01B and a NIM of 2.84%. Schwab is due pre-open ($1.66 / $7.20B). BAC fell ≈5% Wednesday after its $1.2B fine (the OCC's $750M share is a record), and the BKX is ≈12% off its August high.

Metals reversed with yields. Spot gold is +1.2% at ≈$4,150 (Dec ≈$4,174) after Wednesday's settle of $4,108.60, helped by a Bloomberg report that China is buying Treasuries through non-US custodians and by the DXY's slide from 102.9 to ≈102.1. Silver fell 6.1% to $55.88 Wednesday and is back to ≈$56.50. LME copper closed at $14,484.50 (−0.6%), ≈$390 below its September record.

Oil is easing. Brent is ≈$104.3 (−1.7%) and WTI ≈$94.1 (−1%) after Wednesday's settles of $106.06 and $95.09, on reports that Washington may ease sanctions on some shadow-fleet tankers to cut freight rates. Hormuz risk is still rising: a Singapore-flagged container ship sank after a projectile strike. API showed an 11.1M bbl crude draw, and EIA data comes at 11:00 CT because of the holiday delay.

calendar.event: PNC & U.S. Bancorp Q3; TSMC Q3
calendar.why: Both regionals beat on EPS and missed slightly on revenue. PNC's loans +17% y/y show C&I demand is alive, and charge-offs +44% y/y are the line to watch. USB's call is at 8:00 CT.

calendar.event: Charles Schwab Q3; also Prologis, Freeport-McMoRan
calendar.why: Schwab is a read on cash sorting and NII at 5% long rates. FCX is a direct copper read with El Teniente and Centinela disrupted.
Some surveys say +0.6% headline. After a 0.3% core CPI, the PPI components that feed core PCE decide whether Oct hike odds climb back toward 50%.
After August's surge, a firm print supports Goolsbee's overheating worry. A miss would let the flight to quality run.

calendar.event: Initial jobless claims; Empire State & Philly Fed (Oct)
calendar.why: Claims below 200K keep the labor market from giving the Fed cover to wait.

calendar.event: 4-week ($110B) and 8-week ($105B) bill auctions; 20Y & 5Y TIPS sizes announced
calendar.why: Large bill supply sits next to SOFR at 3.89%. The 20Y reopening (Oct 21) and 5Y TIPS (Oct 22) sizes set next week's duration supply.
Confirms or refutes the API draw. The SPR at 283M bbl is the lowest since 1982.

calendar.event: Fed's Hammack (time unconfirmed); Chair Warsh at IMF in Bangkok, 10:30 PM CT
calendar.why: Warsh gets the last word before the Oct 17 blackout. Any validation of an October move would reprice the 2Y overnight.
Opex comes with SKEW at 157 and VIX1D jumping, so dealer hedging can exaggerate moves.
Blackout starts Sat Oct 17. CME and Northern Trust report Oct 21.

rates.title: CPI spike fades as the tech rout bids duration
rates.body: The 10Y hit ≈5.33% after CPI but closed at 5.19% (−2 bp), and it is ≈5.10% this morning, a three-week low. The 2Y round-tripped from ≈4.94% intraday to a 4.81% close and is now 4.74%. Saxo and Newsquawk attribute the reversal to safe-haven buying and stretched shorts covering as AI stocks broke.
rates.simple: A Treasury yield is the interest the government pays to borrow, and it moves opposite to the bond's price. Hot inflation first pushed yields up because traders expected more Fed hikes, then a stock-market scare sent investors running into Treasuries, which pulled yields back down. For borrowers, lower long yields mean slightly cheaper mortgages and corporate loans, at least for now.

rates.title: Fed path: October back to a minority view, December near-locked
rates.body: Oct 28 hike odds swung from >50% intraday Wednesday to ≈30–37% late (FXStreet 31.6%, FNN 37.1%), while December is ≈90%. Commerzbank counts ≈29 bp of hikes by end-2026 and ≈75 bp by end-2027. Goolsbee called CPI 'discouraging' but wants more data, and Bowman and Daly signalled no rush.
rates.simple: Futures markets let traders bet on where the Fed's policy rate will be, and the prices tell you the odds of a hike at each meeting. Fed officials sounded worried about inflation but not ready to act in two weeks, so traders pushed the next hike out to December. That matters because the Fed's rate sets what banks pay on deposits and charge on floating-rate loans.

rates.title: Global yields follow Treasuries lower
rates.body: The Bund 10Y fell ≈6–9 bp to ≈3.38–3.40%, its lowest since Sep 9, and the JGB 10Y dropped ≈5 bp to ≈2.93%, a one-month low. Gilts are lower across the curve. As of Oct 9, the 10Y TIPS real yield was ≈2.87–2.91%, 10Y breakevens 2.33% and the Fed's 10Y term premium ≈1.08%, so most of the 5%+ 10Y is real yield and term premium rather than expected inflation.
rates.simple: Government bond markets around the world move together because big investors can shift money between them. A 'real yield' is what a bond pays after inflation, and 'term premium' is the extra pay investors demand for locking money up for years. With both high, long-term borrowing is expensive mainly because investors want compensation for risk, not because they expect runaway inflation.

derivatives.title: Vol reprices at the front of the curve
derivatives.body: The VIX closed at 16.87 (+10.5%), and VIX1D jumped 31.6% to 14.11, but the term structure stayed in contango with VIX3M at 18.79. SKEW hit 157.3, a 60-session high, and VVIX was 94.5. Saxo's read: front-end vol repriced while longer-dated vol held, so traders are buying crash protection for days, not months.
derivatives.simple: The VIX measures how much traders pay for options that protect against S&P 500 swings. 'Contango' means longer-dated protection still costs more than short-dated, a sign the market sees this as a near-term scare rather than a crisis. A high SKEW reading means people are paying up specifically for insurance against a sharp drop.

derivatives.title: AI credit stress shows up in CDS
derivatives.body: CoreWeave's credit default swaps widened from >600 bp Wednesday to >1,000 bp early today, and its 2032 bonds yield above 15% after a 15% stock drop. That is the derivatives market pricing real default risk in the AI data-center build-out, which runs heavily on debt, and it helped drive the duration bid in Treasury futures.
derivatives.simple: A credit default swap (CDS) is insurance against a company not paying its debts. 1,000 bp means paying about 10% of the debt's value each year for that insurance, a level usually seen at distressed borrowers. When lenders get nervous about a company tied to the AI boom, banks and bond investors who funded data centers start re-checking their exposure.

derivatives.title: CME's record quarter sets up Oct 21 earnings; ICE moves on livestock
derivatives.body: CME posted record September ADV of 31.8M contracts (+22% y/y) and a record Q3 of 29.4M (+16%), with interest-rate products at records. BrokerTec set a single-day record of $1.261T on Sep 30. ICE plans to list live cattle, feeder cattle and lean hog futures from Dec 7, pending approval, which challenges a CME franchise.
derivatives.simple: CME Group runs the Chicago exchange where traders buy and sell futures, contracts to trade something later at a price fixed now. Volatile rates mean more hedging, and CME earns a fee on every contract. ICE launching rival livestock contracts tests whether CME's long hold on that market is as secure as it looks.

metals.title: Gold rebounds above $4,150 as yields and the dollar retreat
metals.body: Spot gold is ≈$4,150–4,159 (+1.2%) and Dec futures ≈$4,174 (+1.6%), recovering from a $4,073 one-week low Wednesday and a Dec settle of $4,108.60 (−1.6%). The drivers are the 10Y's ≈9 bp drop, a DXY back to ≈102.1, and a Bloomberg report that China is buying Treasuries via non-US custodians, which pushed Canada's holdings to nearly $600B.
metals.simple: Gold pays no interest, so it gets more attractive when bond yields fall and when the dollar weakens, which makes gold cheaper for foreign buyers. Both happened overnight, undoing Wednesday's inflation-driven selloff. For banks with precious-metals desks, swings like this drive client hedging and trading revenue.

metals.title: Silver and platinum took the bigger hit
metals.body: Dec silver fell 6.1% to $55.88 Wednesday and is ≈$56.50 (+1.5%) now. Platinum fell ≈3.5% to $1,604, a 10-week low. The industrial-heavy metals fell hardest because hike fears and the AI-equity rout hit growth expectations on top of the dollar move.
metals.simple: Silver and platinum are used heavily in factories and electronics as well as for investment, so they swing more than gold when growth worries rise. A 6% one-day drop is large for a commodity. It shows how fast leveraged positions get flushed out when interest-rate expectations jump.

metals.title: Copper slips from near-record as the dollar peaks; supply risk persists
metals.body: LME 3M closed at $14,484.50/t (−0.6%) Wednesday after touching $14,700, ≈$390 below September's $14,875 record, and aluminium broke below $3,000. LME stocks are 232,275 t. Codelco's El Teniente is partly suspended after a fatal landslide, and a strike at Antofagasta's Centinela adds risk. Central-bank demand underpins gold: the PBOC bought ≈21 t in September, its 23rd straight monthly purchase.
metals.simple: Copper is used in wiring, power grids and data centers, so its price tracks both economic growth and mine supply. Prices dipped because a strong dollar makes metals pricier for most buyers, but problems at big Chilean mines keep supply tight. Freeport-McMoRan reports today and will show how miners are handling it.

banking.title: PNC: EPS beat on loan growth, charge-offs climbing
banking.body: Adjusted EPS was $5.09 ($4.97 reported) vs $4.91, and revenue $6.56B vs $6.61B. NII was $4.2B (+$99M q/q), while fees fell 6% q/q to $2.1B after a strong Q2 in capital markets. Average loans rose 17% y/y on C&I, the efficiency ratio was 57%, and net charge-offs were $257M (+44% y/y).
banking.simple: PNC is a big Pittsburgh-based regional bank, and it makes most of its money from net interest income (the gap between what it earns on loans and pays on deposits). Businesses are borrowing a lot more, which grows that income. The rising loan losses (charge-offs) are the early warning to watch if the economy slows under higher rates.

banking.title: U.S. Bancorp edges past on EPS with BTIG in the numbers
banking.body: EPS was $1.34 vs $1.32, and net revenue $7.97B (+8.7%) vs $8.01B expected, including the BTIG acquisition. NII was $4.47B with a NIM of 2.84%. The provision was $654M and CET1 10.80%, with efficiency at 55.9%.
banking.simple: Net interest margin (NIM) is the bank's profit spread on its loans and deposits, expressed as a percentage. CET1 is the core capital cushion regulators require to absorb losses, so a higher number means a safer bank. USB is buying a trading firm, BTIG, to earn more fee income that doesn't depend on interest rates.

banking.title: BAC fine: OCC's largest ever, with no end date on the order
banking.body: BAC fell ≈5% Wednesday (low $49.44) on adjusted EPS of $1.08 vs $1.10, after a $1.2B AML/sanctions penalty that cost 17¢. The OCC's $750M share is its largest ever, and it covers more than $5B of unreported suspicious transactions. The consent order has no termination date, and bank stocks (BKX) are ≈12% off their mid-August high.
banking.simple: Anti-money-laundering (AML) rules require banks to flag suspicious transfers to the government. Bank of America failed to report billions of dollars of them and is being fined heavily. An open-ended order means regulators will keep watching closely, which can slow the bank's growth plans and raise its compliance costs.

banking.title: Deals: Bumble take-private, Galderma–ZO, IonQ–Elisity
banking.body: Ithaca Holdings is taking Bumble private for $1.3B in cash at $6.05/share, a ≈138% premium. Galderma agreed to buy ZO Skin Health from Blackstone at a $1.5B enterprise value (via the WSJ). Separately, IonQ is buying Elisity for up to $1.3B. We found no new bank M&A in the past 48h; the last was TowneBank buying blueharbor for ≈$154M on Oct 6.
banking.simple: M&A (mergers and acquisitions) is when companies buy each other, and investment banks earn advisory fees and lend money to finance the deals. A 'take-private' means a buyer purchases all public shares so the company stops trading on the stock market. Steady mid-size deals keep bank fee income flowing even when markets are shaky.

banking.title: IPO window: small deals only, Anthropic looms
banking.body: Amaero priced a downsized IPO at $4.25, and BioVentrix pulled its $17M deal. City Therapeutics (≈$175M) and Iambic (≈$150M) are on the calendar, and US IPOs year to date total 115. Per a Reuters digest of the NYT, Anthropic's Q3 revenue rose ≈45% q/q to ≈$16.8B ahead of what could be the largest IPO ever.
banking.simple: An IPO (initial public offering) is when a company first sells shares to the public, with banks underwriting (guaranteeing and selling) the deal for a fee. In shaky markets, smaller IPOs get cut or pulled. A giant listing like Anthropic would be a large fee event for whichever banks lead it.

cnbc.title: AI-chip rout erases more than $1T this week
cnbc.body: The 20 biggest AI/semiconductor names have lost more than $1T this week on rate and AI-funding worries. SK Hynix fell >10%, Samsung 8.7% and SoftBank 7.9%, and pre-market Nvidia was −1.8%, Micron −4.4% and AMD −3.5%.
cnbc.simple: Investors have spent heavily on companies tied to artificial intelligence, often with borrowed money. Higher interest rates make that debt costlier and future profits worth less today, so the stocks are being sold hard. Since these companies are a large share of major indexes, their slide drags down many retirement accounts.

cnbc.title: Ship sinks near Hormuz; oil still eases
cnbc.body: The Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank after an unidentified projectile hit it, and all 21 crew escaped. A second ship was damaged. Dec Brent still fell ≈1.7% to ≈$104.3 and Nov WTI ≈1.1% to ≈$94.05, and the IEA warned that diesel will stay tight into next year.
cnbc.simple: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow channel that carries about a fifth of the world's oil. Attacks there raise the risk premium (the extra price for possible disruption), but reports that the US may relax some sanctions to free up tankers pushed prices down today. Diesel shortages matter because trucking and farming run on it, so they feed into food and goods prices.

cnbc.title: Nasdaq futures slide while the Dow holds up
cnbc.body: Pre-market, NQ futures were ≈−1.1–1.3%, ES ≈−0.3–0.4% and Dow futures ≈+0.3–0.4%. That follows the S&P's −1.11% (7,718.94) and the Nasdaq's −1.88% (26,692.87) Wednesday, the worst day since July.
cnbc.simple: Futures trade before the stock market opens and show where prices are likely to start. The tech-heavy Nasdaq is under pressure, while the Dow, heavier in banks and industrial companies, is holding up. That gap shows money moving out of AI bets into steadier businesses.

cnbc.title: Dollar backs off 18-month high as Fed officials cool October talk
cnbc.body: The DXY slipped to ≈102.1 from ≈102.9 as yields fell. Bowman and Daly said the Fed can wait for more data before Oct 27–28. Reuters had put 'no change' at ≈49% right after CPI, vs 81% before it.
cnbc.simple: The dollar index measures the dollar against major currencies, and it tends to rise when US interest rates are expected to climb. Fed officials hinted they aren't in a hurry, so the dollar gave back some gains. A softer dollar helps US exporters and makes commodities like gold cheaper for buyers abroad.

wsj.title: Netflix cuts ≈1,000 jobs, ≈6% of staff
wsj.body: These are Netflix's biggest cuts since 2022, mostly in product, technology, legal and HR. The WSJ ties them to slower growth and softer engagement.
wsj.simple: Layoffs at a profitable tech company signal that management expects slower growth and wants to protect margins (the profit kept from each dollar of sales). It's part of a broader pattern of big companies trimming staff while spending heavily on AI.

wsj.title: Japan to fund up to $21B of GlobalFoundries fabs in New York
wsj.body: Japan will put up to $21B toward two GlobalFoundries chip plants in New York State, to be jointly owned by US and Japanese interests. GFS rose ≈4.8% to $48.94.
wsj.simple: A 'fab' is a chip factory, and governments are paying to build them at home so they aren't dependent on Asia for chips. Japan funding plants in the US is part of trade-and-investment deals between the two countries. Projects this size need large bank loans and bond deals.

wsj.title: AEP plans ≈$4B fuel-cell plant to power Google
wsj.body: American Electric Power plans ≈$4B of fuel-cell generation in Wyoming, backed by a 20-year power purchase agreement with Google.
wsj.simple: AI data centers need huge amounts of electricity, so tech companies are signing long-term contracts directly with utilities. A 20-year contract makes the project easy to finance with debt, which is steady business for commercial and project-finance banks.

wsj.title: Galderma buys ZO Skin Health from Blackstone
wsj.body: Galderma agreed to acquire ZO Skin Health from Blackstone at a $1.5B enterprise value.
wsj.simple: Private-equity firms like Blackstone buy companies, improve them and then sell them, and this is one of those exits. Enterprise value is the total price including the company's debt. Sales like this return cash to private-equity investors, who then fund new deals that banks help finance.

tribune.title: Rush and Endeavor Health plan to merge into Chicago's largest system
tribune.body: The combined system would have 12 hospitals, 400+ sites, 46,000+ staff and over 2M patients a year under the Rush name, led by Endeavor CEO J.P. Gallagher. Endeavor commits $1B ($300M community, $500M academics/research, $200M quality). The deal needs regulatory approval and targets an early-2027 close.
tribune.simple: Hospital systems merge to cut costs and gain bargaining power with insurers. Regulators check whether the merger would push up prices for patients. A deal this size usually brings bond refinancing and advisory work for banks.

tribune.title: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee: September CPI was 'discouraging'
tribune.body: Goolsbee flagged services inflation and demand overheating tied to AI capex as concerns, but he isn't yet backing a hike and wants more data before Oct 27–28.
tribune.simple: Goolsbee runs the Chicago Fed and votes on interest rates. He is saying inflation is a problem but he won't commit to raising rates yet. Markets read comments like his to guess what the Fed will do in two weeks.

tribune.title: Council falls one vote short of overriding Johnson's borrowing veto
tribune.body: The override failed by one vote, a week before Mayor Johnson presents his plan to close an $882M 2027 budget gap.
tribune.simple: Chicago borrows by selling municipal bonds, and how it handles its budget hole affects its credit rating (a grade for how likely it is to repay). A lower rating means higher interest costs for the city, which taxpayers pay. Muni investors and underwriting banks watch these fights closely.

tribune.title: ICE takes aim at CME's livestock futures
tribune.body: ICE plans to launch live cattle, feeder cattle and lean hog futures, targeting Dec 7 pending regulatory approval, in a direct challenge to CME's long-held dominance (reported Oct 13).
tribune.simple: Ranchers and meatpackers use livestock futures to lock in prices and protect against swings. CME has owned this market for decades. A rival could pressure CME's fees, though traders usually stick with the exchange that already has the most activity.

nyt.title: Anthropic's Q3 revenue ≈$16.8B ahead of possible record IPO
nyt.body: The NYT reports Anthropic's Q3 revenue rose ≈45% q/q to ≈$16.8B, ahead of what could be the biggest IPO on record.
nyt.simple: Anthropic builds AI models and is growing revenue very fast. If it goes public, the banks running the IPO would earn large fees, and it would test whether investors still want AI exposure after this week's selloff.

nyt.title: Iran escalates attacks on shipping near Hormuz
nyt.body: Attacks on vessels near the Strait last week nearly matched all of September's total, and a container ship sank off Oman.
nyt.simple: More attacks make shipping through the Gulf riskier and pricier, which raises insurance and freight costs and eventually what people pay for fuel. That is why oil stays above $100 despite talk of easing sanctions.

nyt.title: Senate Finance probes Meta's $6.6B in R&D tax credits
nyt.body: Senators are questioning Meta's use of federal research tax credits, which total $6.6B over two years and may have cut its tax bill.
nyt.simple: The R&D tax credit lowers taxes for companies that spend on research. Lawmakers want to know whether Meta's claims stretched the rules. Any tightening could raise effective tax rates across Big Tech.

talking_points.topic: Inflation shock vs flight to quality
talking_points.point: In 24 hours the 10Y went from 5.19% to a 5.33% intraday high on core CPI of 0.3%, then to ≈5.10% as AI credit cracked (CoreWeave CDS >1,000 bp). The front end is pricing ≈29 bp of hikes by end-2026 even as the long end rallies. Question for a rates trader: when the inflation and risk-off signals point opposite ways, do you fade the long-end rally into PPI, or position for a bull steepener on the view that credit stress ends the hiking cycle?

talking_points.topic: Regional NII is working, but watch credit
talking_points.point: PNC grew average loans 17% y/y with NII up $99M q/q, and USB holds a 2.84% NIM, while big-bank FICC missed at JPM, BAC and MS. But PNC's charge-offs rose 44% y/y. For a commercial-banking interview: with C&I demand this strong at 5%+ long rates, how much is AI/data-center capex financing, and how is the bank pricing that concentration now that CoreWeave's CDS trades like a distressed name?

talking_points.topic: Gold's tug of war: real yields vs official buying
talking_points.point: Gold fell to $4,073 on CPI and the dollar, then rebounded to ≈$4,150 as the 10Y dropped 9 bp, with the PBOC on its 23rd straight month of buying (≈21 t in September) and global ETFs taking a record $31B in Q3. Silver fell 6.1% in one day. For a metals desk: is the gold–real-yield link back in charge, or does central-bank buying put a floor under gold that makes selling downside puts (low strikes) the better trade?

caveats: WSJ, NYT and the Chicago Tribune were not directly accessible, and several research tools could not open pages directly. WSJ and NYT items come from Reuters' French-language press digests (Boursorama/Zonebourse), and the Chicago bucket uses the Sun-Times, Crain's and Reuters. Most figures are drawn from search-result excerpts, and pre-market levels are approximate with snapshot times varying. Yesterday's Close update showed intraday-spike yields; this brief uses CNBC/Forbes closes. Oct 28 hike odds vary widely by snapshot (≈30–48%). Consensus for PPI headline conflicts (+0.5% vs +0.6%), and Empire/Philly consensus was not found. The MOVE index, palladium and a live copper quote were not confirmed, and real-yield/term-premium figures are as of Oct 9.

updates.label: Close
updates.headline: The rotation stuck into the close: the Dow finished +1.08% at 52,177.69, and Treasuries held most of a ≈10–13 bp rally as the AI-credit scare beat a 6.3% PPI. CoreWeave flipped to a gain once Nvidia's Huang backed it, so the panic is easing in stocks but not in its bonds.
points: Close: Dow 52,177.69 (+556 pts, +1.08%; it had been −1.4% intraday), S&P 500 7,744.06 (+0.33%), Nasdaq 26,713.03 (+0.08%) (Yahoo/CNBC closing tables). The Nasdaq erased a ≈−1.3% early loss. The Russell 2000 is still in correction, ≈11% below its Aug 14 record after Wed's −1.93% to 2,729.53. I found no confirmed Thu close for it.

Rates: the 10Y ended the day near 5.06–5.10% (Bloomberg 5.06%, −13 bp; Trading Economics 5.10%, −9 bp) and the 2Y near 4.72–4.73% (≈−8 bp), the biggest one-day drop for the 10Y since Aug 2025. Late in the day yields bounced a little off their lows. Oct 28 hike odds are ≈30%, down from a 58% post-CPI peak (ZeroHedge/CME). European, UK, Japanese and Australian yields fell as much as 10 bp alongside.

Commodities: Comex gold settled ≈$4,147.70 (+1.54%), snapping a three-day losing streak, and silver +2.3% (no settlement print found). WTI Nov settled $97.97 (+$2.88) after EIA showed a −8.6M bbl crude draw vs ≈−0.3M expected, while Brent Dec settled $105.92 (−$0.14) on talk of US sanctions relief for shadow-fleet tankers (Newsquawk). That narrowed the Brent–WTI spread to ≈$8. Copper was ≈−1.2% late morning at $6.58/lb (Mining.com), its third straight drop.

AI credit: CRWV went from −9.5% to roughly +3% to +6% (≈$67.7–69.7) after Jensen Huang said its finances are improving. Deutsche Bank called the sell-off a buying chance. Its bonds were mixed: one feed had the 2030s +5.7c to 91.3, but the 9.75% 2031s yielded ≈15.8% and the 5Y CDS hit a record ≈1,195 bp intraday. Stocks recovered faster than the credit did.

Morning thesis check: the morning call that PPI would decide the front end was wrong. The flight to quality won, though PPI's +0.7% core will still feed into core PCE. Tonight 10:30 PM CT: Warsh at the IMF in Bangkok, the last word before the Sat blackout. Fri: Truist Q3, Sep import prices (7:30 CT) and industrial production (8:15 CT), plus monthly options expiration with SKEW elevated.
updates.simple: Investors kept moving money out of AI and chip stocks and into Treasuries and "old-economy" stocks like industrials and banks. That buying pushed long-term Treasury yields (the interest the government pays to borrow) down sharply, even though a key wholesale inflation number came in very hot. Lower yields lifted gold, which pays no interest. Oil's U.S. benchmark jumped because U.S. crude stockpiles fell far more than expected. For banks and borrowers, mortgage and corporate loan rates (which track the 10-year) got a little cheaper today. The Fed may still raise rates on Oct 28, but traders now see that as less likely than not.

updates.label: Midday
updates.headline: At midday the rotation is holding. The 10Y is near 5.08% (≈−10 bp) and the Dow is up ≈0.9%, but CoreWeave hit a new low and tech lags, so the market is still trading AI credit rather than the 6.3% PPI.
points: Stocks ≈11:00–11:15 CT: Dow ≈52,070 (+0.9%), S&P ≈7,728 (+0.1%), Nasdaq ≈26,609 (−0.3%; 24/7 Wall St had it −1.1% at noon ET). XLF is +0.85% and IWM +0.7%: money is moving out of AI/chips into banks, value and small caps. The S&P has recovered from the ≈−0.3% early dip.

Rates: the 10Y is ≈5.07–5.09% and the 30Y ≈5.43%, per CNBC/Reuters. That puts the 10Y on track for its biggest one-day drop since Aug 2025. The 2Y is ≈4.76% (−5 bp), so the curve is bull-flattening (long yields falling faster): 2s10s ≈32 bp vs ≈37 bp at Wed close. Bills: the 4-wk stopped at 4.000% (BTC 2.56) and the 8-wk at 4.050% (BTC 2.26), per an aggregator, not yet verified with Treasury. Both are at or above the 4.00% top of the funds range, so the bill market is still pricing hike risk for Oct 28/Dec 9.

AI credit: CoreWeave is ≈−9% at ≈$59.8, below its $60.56 prior 52-week low, for a 4th straight loss. Mizuho cut its target to $88 from $115. The company has ≈$50B of debt, and its 2031/2032 notes yielded ≈14.8–14.9% on Wed.

Metals: gold is ≈$4,154–4,159 (+1.2–1.3%; Kitco day range $4,099–4,169) as real yields fall. Silver is ≈$57.25 (+2.5%), which has now made back about 40% of Wed's 6% drop. COMEX copper is ≈$6.57/lb (−1.4%), pressured by hot inflation data and the preliminary Escondida deal that averts a strike.

Banks: USB beat on EPS ($1.34 vs $1.32) but revenue was $7.97B vs $7.99B. It raised FY26 revenue and operating-leverage guidance and sees net interest margin (NIM) heading toward 3% in 2027. Correction to the calendar: FCX's full Q3 report is Oct 27, not today (its Oct 2 update already showed ≈830M lb of copper). EIA crude: one feed shows −8.6M bbl vs −0.2M expected. That is unconfirmed, and there is no reliable fresh WTI/Brent print.
updates.simple: Investors are selling AI and chip stocks, worried that heavily indebted AI companies like CoreWeave can't keep borrowing at high rates. They are putting the money into Treasuries and "boring" stocks like banks and industrials instead. That buying pushes Treasury yields (the interest a bond pays) down, which helps gold, because gold pays no interest and looks better when bonds pay less. Short-term Treasury bills still pay above the Fed's current range, though, so traders haven't ruled out a Fed rate hike this month.

updates.label: Post-open
updates.headline: September PPI blew out (+1.3% m/m, core +0.7%) and retail sales beat (+0.8%), yet the AI-credit flight to quality wins: the 10Y is still ≈11 bp lower at ≈5.08% and October hike odds are stuck near 31%.
points: PPI (Sep): headline +1.3% m/m vs ≈0.5% consensus and +6.3% y/y vs 5.3%, the largest annual gain since 2022. Core was +0.7% vs 0.3% (5.0% y/y vs 4.4%). Per BLS, energy (+10.8%) drove more than 80% of the headline jump. This is worse than the morning 'hot' scenario.

Retail sales: +0.8% vs +0.3% expected, with August revised up to +1.3%. Ex-gas stations sales rose only +0.2%, so much of the beat is fuel prices, not volume. Claims came in at ≈199K vs 195K expected.

Rates ignored the data: the 2Y is 4.75% (≈−6 bp) and the 10Y ≈5.07–5.09% (≈−11 to −13 bp, per CNBC), and Oct 28 hike pricing is ≈31%. The morning's 'hot PPI undoes the rally' call was wrong. For now the market treats the AI-credit unwind (CoreWeave ≈−14%, its bond yields ≈15%) as the bigger risk than energy-led pipeline inflation.

Stocks are split: early on the Dow is ≈+0.6% while the S&P is ≈−0.3% and the Nasdaq ≈−0.8%. Gold is $4,144.60 (Kitco 8:53 ET), back above Wed's CPI loss as yields fall, and silver is ≈$56.70 (+1.9%). WTI is ≈$94.8 (−0.3%).

Schwab: adj. EPS $1.69 vs $1.66 on revenue of $7.17B vs $7.20B, with a record $190.4B in core net new assets (+38% y/y) and $13.33T in client assets. The stock was ≈−1% to −4% pre-market, the same pattern as PNC/USB: EPS beats, light revenue. EIA crude data is at 11:00 CT.
updates.simple: The producer price index (what businesses charge each other, an early read on future consumer prices) jumped far more than expected, mostly because of energy. Normally that pushes bond yields (the interest a bond pays) up, since it makes a Fed rate hike more likely. Today yields fell anyway, because investors scared by losses in AI-linked companies are buying Treasuries for safety. For banks and borrowers, that means long-term borrowing costs are easing even as inflation runs hot, and that tension has to break one way before the Oct 28 Fed meeting.
